content: Cleft palate is the most common congenital facial deformity, and it can significantly impact speech development. This condition often leads to articulation errors, which may persist into adulthood if not properly addressed. Electropalatography (EPG) is a technique that has been utilized in speech therapy for individuals whose articulation problems do not respond to conventional treatment methods. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness of speech therapy interventions using EPG in treating articulation errors in individuals with repaired cleft palate. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, and PsycINFO, covering literature up to March 2008. Additionally, specific journals such as Clinical Linguistics and Phonetics, Cleft Palate Journal/Cleft Palate-Craniofacial Journal, and the International Journal of Language and Communication Disorders were hand-searched. The EPG bibliography by Gibbon (2007) was also reviewed, and researchers were contacted to identify any other relevant published or unpublished studies. The selection criteria for this review included randomized controlled trials that compared EPG-based interventions to no treatment, delayed treatment, standard treatment, or alternative therapeutic approaches for managing articulation disorders in children or adults with cleft palate. Data collection and analysis involved one author screening titles and abstracts and assessing the quality of trials, with a second author verifying these judgments. Disagreements were resolved through discussion, and three authors were available to evaluate potential trials for inclusion. Only one trial met the inclusion criteria for this review. This study employed a parallel design and reported that fewer therapy sessions were required to achieve treatment goals when using EPG therapy combined with a frication display method, followed by EPG therapy alone, and then standard treatment. However, no meta-analysis was performed due to the limited data. The authors concluded that the included trial was small in scale and had significant methodological limitations. These included unclear allocation concealment, lack of blinding of outcome assessors, limited use of quantitative outcome measures, and deviations from the planned reporting of results. Consequently, the current evidence supporting the efficacy of EPG for treating articulation disorders in individuals with cleft palate is weak. There is a clear need for high-quality randomized controlled trials to further investigate the potential benefits of EPG in this area.
